data.appendix_basis: Appendix J(c)(1), Example (i): Monthly payments (regular first period).  ([Federal Reserve][1])

inputs.payment_schedule: 24 monthly payments of $230; advance 1-10-78; first payment 2-10-78

data.unit_period_analysis: The common period is 1 month, so the unit-period is 1 month and w = 12 unit-periods per year. From 1-10-78 to 2-10-78 is exactly 1 unit-period, so t = 1 and f = 0. ([Federal Reserve][1])

data.case_name: Single-advance, single-payment transaction (255-day term)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J(c)(5), Example (i): Single-advance, single-payment, term less than one year measured in days. ([Federal Reserve][1])

inputs.payment_schedule: One payment of $1,080; advance 1-3-78; payment 9-15-78

data.unit_period_analysis: The term is 255 days, less than one year and not a whole number of months. Appendix J therefore makes the unit-period the term itself: 1 unit-period = 255 days, with w = 365/255. The entire term is one unit-period, so t = 1 and f = 0. ([Federal Reserve][1])

data.fact_pattern: An MNE Group in Jurisdiction X has GloBE Income of 200 in Year 1 and 100 in Year 2. data.computation: GloBE Income: EUR 1,000 − EUR 50 allocable to non-Group Entities = EUR 950; EUR 950 − EUR 500 allocated to the PE = EUR 450 allocated to B Co 2. Payroll: EUR 200 × 50% = EUR 100 allocated to the PE; EUR 200 × 45% = EUR 90 allocated to B Co 2; EUR 200 − EUR 100 − EUR 90 = EUR 10 not included in a Constituent Entity's SBIE. Tangible Assets: EUR 400 × 50% = EUR 200 allocated to the PE; EUR 400 × 45% = EUR 180 allocated to B Co 2; EUR 400 − EUR 200 − EUR 180 = EUR 20 not included in a Constituent Entity's SBIE.

data.fact_pattern: B Co was created July 1 of Year 1. Year 1 GloBE Revenue = EUR 1 million and GloBE Income = EUR 50,000 over six months. Year 2 GloBE Revenue = EUR 1 million and GloBE Income = EUR 100,000. Year 3 GloBE Revenue = EUR 3 million and GloBE Loss = EUR 200,000.

Three-year Average GloBE Revenue = (EUR 2 million + EUR 1 million + EUR 3 million) / 3 = EUR 2 million. Three-year Average GloBE Income/Loss = (EUR 100,000 + EUR 100,000 − EUR 200,000) / 3 = EUR 0.
data.result: Average GloBE Revenue is EUR 2 million, below EUR 10 million, and Average GloBE Income/Loss is EUR 0, below EUR 1 million. Therefore, if elected by the Filing Constituent Entity, Top-up Tax for B Co is deemed to be zero for Year 3.
data.weakest_point: The document phrases the second threshold as Average GloBE Income or Loss being less than EUR 1 million; the arithmetic result is exactly EUR 0. ([OECD][1])

data.fact_pattern: A Co first becomes subject to the GloBE Rules for the fiscal year ending December 31, 2023. Country A has a 20% corporate income tax rate. In 2022 A Co earned EUR 100 of interest income subject to EUR 30 of foreign withholding tax; EUR 20 was usable as a tax credit and EUR 10 was carried forward, with a EUR 10 deferred tax asset. A Co also received a EUR 10 investment tax credit and recorded a EUR 10 deferred tax asset.
data.computation: For each EUR 10 tax-credit deferred tax asset: EUR 10 / 20% = EUR 50 of underlying tax-effected amount; EUR 50 × 15% Minimum Rate = EUR 7.5. Thus the foreign-tax-credit carry-forward DTA is recast from EUR 10 to EUR 7.5, and the investment-tax-credit carry-forward DTA is likewise recast from EUR 10 to EUR 7.5. Total recast DTA = EUR 7.5 + EUR 7.5 = EUR 15.
data.result: Both tax-credit carry-forward deferred tax assets are taken into account in the Transition Year and subsequent years and are each recast to EUR 7.5 at the 15% Minimum Rate.
data.weakest_point: The example contains two separate EUR 10 deferred tax assets, and the recast formula is applied independently to each; the key directional rule is recasting to the 15% Minimum Rate rather than retaining the 20% domestic rate. ([OECD][1])

data.fact_pattern: A Constituent Entity accrues in 2023 a disallowed deferred tax asset of EUR 1,000, recorded at or below the Minimum Rate, with no recast. It records EUR 100 of deferred tax expense from reversal of that DTA in each year from 2024 through 2033. Profit before tax is EUR 2,000 in each of 2024–2026. Simplified Covered Taxes before adjustment are EUR 300, EUR 320 and EUR 340 respectively, consisting of current tax of EUR 200, EUR 220 and EUR 240 plus EUR 100 deferred tax expense each year.
data.computation: Original DTA = EUR 1,000. Grace Period Limitation = 20% × EUR 1,000 = EUR 200. 2024: EUR 100 deferred tax expense is allowable because EUR 100 ≤ EUR 200; Simplified Covered Taxes = EUR 300; Simplified ETR = EUR 300 / EUR 2,000 = 15%. 2025: cumulative allowable deferred tax expense = EUR 100 + EUR 100 = EUR 200, still equal to the limitation; Simplified Covered Taxes = EUR 320; Simplified ETR = EUR 320 / EUR 2,000 = 16%. 2026: Grace Period has ended, so the EUR 100 deferred tax expense is excluded; Simplified Covered Taxes = EUR 340 − EUR 100 = EUR 240; Simplified ETR = EUR 240 / EUR 2,000 = 12%.
data.result: The Grace Period is 2024 and 2025, with a EUR 200 limitation. The jurisdiction qualifies for the Transitional CbCR Safe Harbour in 2024 and 2025, but not in 2026; the jurisdiction's Transition Year is consequently 2026.
data.weakest_point: The example's conclusion concerns eligibility for the Transitional CbCR Safe Harbour rather than a direct top-up-tax computation; the 2026 12% ETR is mechanically implied by the stated EUR 240 adjusted taxes and EUR 2,000 profit. ([OECD][1])

data.computation: 10% bucket LE sum = 400 + 100 + 50 = $550. 10% threshold = $550 × 0.10 = $55. Permitted aggregate CD amount = $550 + $55 = $605. 10% bucket CD sum = 500 + 80 + 50 = $630. The individual increase on the settlement-agent fee is $100, which is more than 10% of that individual $400 fee, but that is not the test: the rule compares aggregate CD charges with aggregate LE charges. Zero-tolerance appraisal: $500 CD ≤ $500 LE, so no violation. No-limit attorney: no tolerance violation merely from the $150 increase, assuming the off-list consumer-selected-service conditions and best-information requirement are satisfied.
data.clause_basis: 12 CFR 1026.19(e)(3)(ii)(A): the aggregate amount of covered third-party-service and recording-fee charges may not exceed the aggregate LE amount by more than 10%. Official commentary expressly says the test remains aggregate even when an individual charge increases by more than 10%. Zero-tolerance charges are governed by §1026.19(e)(3)(i), while consumer-selected providers not on the creditor's list fall under §1026.19(e)(3)(iii)(D). ([Consumer Financial Protection Bureau][1]) 
data.weakest_point: The no-limit classification assumes the attorney was a required service for which the consumer selected a provider not on the creditor's list and the original estimate satisfied the best-information requirement.

The required comparison is $1,130 aggregate CD versus $1,000 aggregate LE. Zero-tolerance underwriting fee: $825 − $800 = $25 violation. No-limit pest inspection: no tolerance violation if it satisfies §1026.19(e)(3)(iii).

([Consumer Financial Protection Bureau][1]) 

data.weakest_point: The no-limit inspection classification assumes the consumer selected a provider not on the creditor's written list and the estimate otherwise met the best-information requirement.

data.case_name: Omitted 10% fee but aggregate remains within tolerance
data.computation: 10% bucket LE sum = $700 + $300 + $0 = $1,000. 10% threshold = $1,000 × 0.10 = $100. Permitted aggregate CD amount = $1,100. 10% bucket CD sum = $760 + $300 + $20 = $1,080. data.clause_basis: Official interpretation of §1026.19(e)(3)(ii)-2 expressly permits an omitted charge in the 10% category to be imposed at consummation so long as the aggregate CD charges do not exceed the aggregate LE charges by more than 10%. ([Consumer Financial Protection Bureau][1])

data.case_name: Single Blocked Person – Simple Indirect Chain (FAQ 401 Example 1)
data.computation:
1. X owns 50% of A directly. Under the 50% Rule, A is blocked because X owns ≥50% of A.
2. Because A is blocked (and A owns 50% of B), X is considered to indirectly own 50% of B through A.
3. Alternatively, the indirect ownership is calculated as: X's ownership of A (50%) × A's ownership of B (50%) = 25%? No — OFAC does not multiply. Since A is ≥50%-owned by X, A is blocked, and A's 50% stake in B is attributed fully to X. Thus X's indirect ownership in B = 50%.
4. Aggregate ownership of B by blocked persons = 50% (indirect via A).

blocked_verdicts.B: Blocked (50% indirect ownership by X through A).

data.guidance_basis: FAQ 401, Example 1. OFAC states: 'Blocked Person X owns 50 percent of Entity A, and Entity A owns 50 percent of Entity B. Entity B is considered to be blocked. This is so because Blocked Person X owns, indirectly, 50% of Entity B.'
data.weakest_point: The calculation does not multiply percentages (50% × 50% = 25%) because the intermediary (A) is itself blocked; the attribution is full.

data.case_name: Single Blocked Person – Convergent Paths (FAQ 401 Example 2)
data.computation:
1. X owns 50% of A directly → A is blocked.
2. X owns 50% of B directly → B is blocked.
3. Because A is blocked, X is considered to indirectly own 25% of C through A (A's 25% stake in C is attributed to X).
4. Because B is blocked, X is considered to indirectly own another 25% of C through B (B's 25% stake in C is attributed to X).
5. Total indirect ownership of C by X = 25% + 25% = 50%.
6. Aggregate ownership of C by blocked persons = 50%.

blocked_verdicts.C: Blocked (50% aggregate indirect ownership by X through A and B; also blocked due to 50% aggregate ownership by blocked entities A and B).

data.guidance_basis: FAQ 401, Example 2. OFAC states: 'Blocked Person X owns 50 percent of Entity A and 50 percent of Entity B. Entities A and B each own 25 percent of Entity C. Entity C is considered to be blocked. This is so because, through its 50 percent ownership of Entity A, Blocked Person X is considered to indirectly own 25 percent of Entity C; and through its 50 percent ownership of Entity B, Blocked Person X is considered to indirectly own another 25 percent of Entity C. When Blocked Person X's indirect ownership of Entity C through Entity A and Entity B is totaled, it equals 50 percent.'
data.weakest_point: The convergent paths are summed (25% + 25% = 50%), not multiplied or averaged.

data.case_name: Single Blocked Person – Mixed Direct and Indirect (FAQ 401 Example 3)
data.computation:
1. X owns 50% of A directly → A is blocked.
2. Because A is blocked, X is considered to indirectly own 40% of B through A (A's 40% stake in B is attributed to X).
3. X also directly owns 10% of B.
4. Total ownership of B by X = direct 10% + indirect 40% = 50%.
5. Aggregate ownership of B by blocked persons = 50%.

blocked_verdicts.B: Blocked (50% aggregate direct and indirect ownership by X).

data.guidance_basis: FAQ 401, Example 3. OFAC states: 'Blocked Person X owns 50 percent of Entity A and 10 percent of Entity B. Entity A also owns 40 percent of Entity B. Entity B is considered to be blocked. This is so because, through its 50 percent ownership of Entity A, Blocked Person X is considered to indirectly own 40 percent of Entity B. When added to Blocked Person X's direct 10 percent ownership of Entity B, Blocked Person X's total ownership (direct and indirect) of Entity B is 50 percent.'
data.weakest_point: The indirect ownership through A is attributed fully (40%), not multiplied (50% × 40% = 20%), because A is blocked.

data.case_name: Multiple Blocked Persons – Aggregate Direct Ownership (FAQ 399)
data.computation:
1. X owns 25% of Z directly.
2. Y owns 25% of Z directly.
3. Aggregate ownership of Z by blocked persons = 25% + 25% = 50%.

blocked_verdicts.Z: Blocked (50% aggregate direct ownership by X and Y).

data.guidance_basis: FAQ 399. OFAC states: 'if Blocked Person X owns 25 percent of Entity A, and Blocked Person Y owns another 25 percent of Entity A, Entity A is considered to be blocked. This is so because Entity A is owned 50 percent or more in the aggregate by one or more blocked persons.'
data.weakest_point: The ownership interests of blocked persons under different sanctions programs are aggregated.

data.case_name: Convergent Paths with Non-Blocked Intermediary (FAQ 401 Example 4)
data.computation:
1. X owns 50% of A directly → A is blocked.
2. Because A is blocked, X is considered to indirectly own 25% of C through A (A's 25% stake in C is attributed to X).
3. X owns 25% of B directly. Since X does not own ≥50% of B, B is not blocked.
4. Because B is not blocked, X is NOT considered to indirectly own any of C through B. The 25% stake that B holds in C is not attributed to X.
5. Total indirect ownership of C by X = 25% (through A) + 0% (through B) = 25%.
6. Aggregate ownership of C by blocked persons = 25%.

blocked_verdicts.B: Not blocked (25% ownership by X, below 50%).
blocked_verdicts.C: Not blocked (25% aggregate indirect ownership by X, below 50%).

data.guidance_basis: FAQ 401, Example 4. OFAC states: 'Blocked Person X owns 50 percent of Entity A and 25 percent of Entity B. Entities A and B each own 25 percent of Entity C. Entity C is not considered to be blocked. This is so because, even though Blocked Person X is considered to indirectly own 25 percent of Entity C through its 50 percent ownership of Entity A, Entity B is not 50 percent or more owned by Blocked Person X, and therefore Blocked Person X is not considered to indirectly own any of Entity C through its part ownership of Entity B. Blocked Person X's total ownership (direct and indirect) of Entity C therefore does not equal or exceed 50 percent.'
data.weakest_point: The crucial point is that indirect ownership is only recognized through intermediaries that are themselves ≥50% owned by blocked persons. A non-blocked intermediary does not pass through ownership for the 50% Rule.

data.case_name: Single Advance, Single Payment (Section (c)(2) Example)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to Part 1026, Section (c)(2)(i)
data.unit_period_analysis: The unit period is 1 year. The number of unit periods from advance to payment is unit_period = 1, with no fractional unit period.
data.computation: Actuarial equation: Amount Financed = Payment / (1 + i)^1, where i is the periodic rate. $1000.00 = $1060.00 / (1 + i)^1 => 1 + i = 1.060 => i = 0.06 or 6.00%. Annual Percentage Rate (APR) = periodic rate * number of unit periods per year = 6.00% * 1 = 6.00%.
data.weakest_point: Simplest possible case; does not test complex fractional unit-period fractions.

data.case_name: Regular Monthly Payment Schedule (Section (c)(1) Example)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to Part 1026, Section (c)(1)
data.unit_period_analysis: The interval between payments is equal (1 month). The unit period is defined as 1 month. The number of unit periods per year (w) is 12. First period is equal to the unit period (fractional period f = 0, full periods t = 1).
data.computation: Actuarial equation: A = P * [(1 - (1 + i)^-n) / i], where A = 5000.00, P = 439.43, n = 12. Solving 5000 = 439.43 * [(1 - (1 + i)^-12) / i] yields monthly periodic rate i = 0.00833333 (0.833333%). Annual Percentage Rate (APR) = 12 * i = 12 * 0.833333% = 10.00%.
data.weakest_point: Standard level repayment amortization; does not exercise odd day formulas.

data.case_name: Irregular First Period with Odd Days (Long First Period)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to Part 1026, Section (b)(5) and (c)(3)
data.unit_period_analysis: Unit period is 1 month (30 days by Appendix J standard month rules or exact days depending on calculation method; using standard unit period = 1 month = 30 days). The first period is 45 days. Number of full unit periods (t) = 1, fractional period (f) = 15/30 = 0.5.
data.computation: Actuarial equation: A = sum [ P_k / ((1 + f*i) * (1 + i)^(k-1)) ]. Here A = 1000.00, P_k = 90.00 for k = 1..12, f = 0.5. 1000 = sum_{k=1}^{12} [ 90 / ((1 + 0.5*i) * (1 + i)^(k-1)) ]. Solving for monthly rate i gives i ≈ 0.0117025. APR = 12 * i = 14.043% rounded to nearest quarter of 1% or 0.1% per Regulation Z (14.04% or 14.0%).
data.weakest_point: Counting convention for odd days in fractional first period (exact day count vs. 30-day month convention under Appendix J rules).

data.case_name: Irregular Payment Schedule (Balloon Payment)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to Part 1026, Section (c)(4)
data.unit_period_analysis: Unit period is 1 month. All intervals are regular unit periods (1 month each, no fractional periods). total periods n = 24.
data.computation: Actuarial equation: A = sum_{k=1}^{23} [ 110 / (1 + i)^k ] + [ 9000 / (1 + i)^24 ]. For A = 10000, solving for i yields monthly rate i ≈ 0.0063284 (0.63284%). Annual Percentage Rate (APR) = 12 * i = 7.594% -> rounded to nearest 0.125% or 0.1% as required by Reg Z = 7.59%.
data.weakest_point: Numerical iteration step for non-standard payment stream.

Step 4: Jurisdictional Top-up Tax = Top-up Tax Percentage * Excess Profit = 5.0% * €100,000,000 = €5,000,000.

Path 2 indirect interest = 60.0% * 50.0% = 30.0%. 3. Total aggregate ownership in Target_C = Path 1 + Path 2 = 20.0% + 30.0% = 50.0%. Since total aggregate ownership is 50.0% (>= 50%), Target_C is blocked.

data.case_name: Regular monthly transaction — 48 equal payments, regular first period
data.appendix_basis: 12 CFR 1026, Appendix J(b) (section letter per best recall) — actuarial-method equation A + Σ_i P_i(1+I)^(-t_i) = 0, unit-period = 1 month → 12 unit-periods per year, APR = 100 × I × 12 (nominal annualization). The equation/unit-period machinery is Appendix J's; the numeric values below are constructed, not reproduced from Appendix J.

inputs.payment_schedule: 48 monthly payments of USD 263.34, first due exactly 1 month after the advance (regular first period)

data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = interval between contractual payment dates = 1 month; 12 unit-periods per year. All intervals regular, so t_i = i (1…48), measured in unit-periods from the advance; no fractional unit-periods arise. I = unit-period (monthly) rate; APR = 100 × I × 12, i.e. nominal annualization, not (1+I)^12 − 1.
data.weakest_point: Whether Appendix J itself prescribes a final rounding step (nearest 1/8 of 1 percentage point) versus leaving accuracy to the §1026.22 tolerances — I state both; the actuarial equation, 12 unit-periods/year for monthly, and nominal annualization (APR = 12 × I) I am confident of; the 10,000 / 48 × 263.34 numbers are mine.

data.case_name: Irregular (short) first period with odd days — 12 monthly payments
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J(c) irregular-transaction rules (section letter per best recall) — an irregular first period is counted in days and expressed as a fractional unit-period (days in the fractional period ÷ days in the unit-period), which enters the exponent t directly. Rule content recalled; numeric example constructed.

inputs.payment_schedule: 12 payments of USD 88.56 on the 5th of each month; advance Jan 15 → first payment Feb 5 (21 days after advance), last payment Jan 5 of the following year

data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month, 12 per year. The 21-day first interval is SHORTER than a unit-period → the first period is a fractional unit-period: 21 days ÷ 31 days (actual days in the corresponding full period Jan 15→Feb 15) = 0.6774194. Exponents: t_i = 0.6774194 + (i−1) → 0.6774, 1.6774, 2.6774, …, 11.6774. Later intervals (Feb 5→Mar 5 etc.) remain 1 unit-period each even though their day counts vary (28/31) — unit-periods are contractual intervals, not day counts; only the odd days are converted to a fraction.
data.result_apr: 12.0000% on the exact payment (88.5640); 11.9908% after cents-rounding to 88.56 → disclosed 12.000% under nearest-1/8 rounding (two-decimal rounding would print 11.99%)
data.weakest_point: The day-count basis for the fractional unit-period: I used 21 ÷ 31 (actual days of the corresponding full month); if Appendix J prescribes a standardized divisor (e.g., 30 days → t₁ = 0.70), the payment shifts ~2¢ and the APR a few bp, and for LONG first periods the choice matters more — I cannot certify the exact basis, nor that this numeric example is published.

data.case_name: Single-advance, single-payment transaction — 182-day note
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J definitions of 'unit-period' and 'number of unit-periods per year' plus its single-payment instructions (section letter uncertain to me) — recalled rule: with a single payment date the unit-period is the advance-to-payment interval, and for non-standard intervals the per-year count = 365 ÷ days in the unit-period. Numeric example constructed.

inputs.payment_schedule: single payment of USD 1,100.00 due 182 days after the advance

data.unit_period_analysis: No recurring contractual payment dates → per the recalled single-payment rule the unit-period is the entire advance-to-payment interval (182 days), so t = 1 exactly and no fractional-unit-period question arises. Unit-periods per year = 365 ÷ 182 = 2.0054945. APR = 100 × I × 2.0054945.
data.computation:
Step 1 — Equation: 1,000 × (1+I)^1 = 1,100 (Appendix J sign form: 1,000 + 1,100×(1+I)^(-1) = 0).
Step 2 — Closed form, no iteration: (1+I) = 1,100/1,000 = 1.100000 → I = 0.100000 per 182-day unit-period.
Step 3 — Annualization count: 365 ÷ 182 = 2.0054945.
Step 4 — APR = 0.100000 × 2.0054945 = 0.2005495 → 20.0549%.
Step 5 — Contrast showing the unit-period definition drives the answer: if the note were instead measured in monthly unit-periods (t = 6), I = 1.10^(1/6) − 1 = 1.6012%/month → APR = 12 × 1.6012% = 19.2142%.
data.weakest_point: Direction-of-rule risk on the unit-period definition: my recall is that a single-payment transaction's unit-period spans the whole advance-to-payment term (corroborated by payday-style APRs = fee% × 365/term, e.g. 15 per 100 over 14 days → 391.07%); if that is wrong and t is measured in months, the answer is 19.21% not 20.05%. Also unsure the divisor is exactly 365 ÷ days (leap-year handling unknown).

data.case_name: Irregular payment amounts — 11 level payments plus a balloon
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J(b) actuarial equation with payment-specific P_i — unequal amounts are handled by summing each P_i at its own exponent t_i. Numeric example constructed (balloon back-solved from a 12% target); does not reproduce any published Appendix J figures.

inputs.payment_schedule: months 1–11: USD 500.00 each; month 12: USD 5,427.00 (balloon); regular monthly intervals, regular first period

data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month, 12 per year; timing is regular so t_i = i (1…12). The irregularity is in the AMOUNTS P_i, which the equation accommodates by summing each payment at its own exponent. No fractional unit-periods.
data.weakest_point: The measurement point of t_i — Appendix J's phrasing may be 'from the beginning of the first payment period' rather than 'from the advance'; identical here only because the first period is regular. The balloon was back-solved from a 12% target, so the example verifies by construction rather than reproducing a published figure.

data.case_name: Irregular payment schedule — skipped month 6 (deferred payment)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J(b)/(c): exponents t_i count ELAPSED unit-periods from the advance, so a gap in the schedule is carried in t, not in payment numbering. Rule content recalled; numeric example constructed (payment back-solved from a 12% target).

inputs.payment_schedule: 11 payments of USD 969.65 due at months 1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10,11,12 — no payment due in month 6 per the original contract; regular first period

data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month, 12 per year; t_i counts elapsed unit-periods from the advance, so payments after the gap carry t = 7…12 even though they are only the 6th–11th payments made. Exponent set: {1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10,11,12}. No fractional periods (regular first period).
data.weakest_point: I assume the month-6 gap is part of the ORIGINAL contractual schedule, so the t_i framework applies unchanged; if the deferral arose from a later modification/forbearance, the original-schedule premise — and possibly the amount financed — would differ. The time-based exponent treatment itself I am confident of.

data.fact_pattern: UPE in Jurisdiction A; a CE in Jurisdiction B. Averages run over the current fiscal year plus the two preceding years (Art 4.1.1). GloBE Revenue of the B CE: Year 1 EUR 9.4m, Year 2 EUR 10.6m, Year 3 EUR 9.2m. GloBE Income: Year 1 EUR 1.6m, Year 2 EUR (0.4)m (a GloBE Loss), Year 3 EUR 0.5m. Thresholds: EUR 10m average GloBE Revenue and EUR 1m average GloBE Income.
data.computation:
Step 1 (revenue average): 9.4 + 10.6 + 9.2 = 29.2; 29.2 / 3 = 9.733333, i.e. ~EUR 9.73m < EUR 10m -> revenue threshold met.
Step 2 (income average; the GloBE Loss year is taken as zero per Art 4.1.2): 1.6 + 0 + 0.5 = 2.1; 2.1 / 3 = 0.700000 = EUR 0.70m < EUR 1m -> income threshold met.
Step 3: both conditions satisfied -> De Minimis Exclusion applies to the CE(s) in Jurisdiction B for the current fiscal year.
data.result: De Minimis Exclusion applies in Jurisdiction B; no top-up tax is computed for B for that year.
data.weakest_point: The exact annual revenue/income figures are my reconstruction - I am confident the document contains a de minimis example applying the loss-as-zero treatment (Art 4.1.2) and requiring BOTH the EUR 10m revenue and EUR 1m income averages to pass, but not of the published numbers (the published example may even include a contrasting jurisdiction that fails).

data.article: Articles 5.1-5.2 (Substance-Based Income Exclusion) with Article 9.2 transitional carve-out rates
data.fact_pattern: FY2023. CE in Jurisdiction C: GloBE Income EUR 100m; Covered Taxes EUR 10m (ETR 10%); eligible payroll EUR 40m; carrying value of eligible tangible assets EUR 60m. Art 9.2.1 transitional rates for 2023: payroll 9.8% (glides down 0.2pp per year from 10% in 2022 toward 5% by 2047); tangible assets 7.8% (glides down 0.2pp per year from 8% in 2022 toward 5% by 2037).
data.computation:
Step 1 (payroll carve-out): 40 x 9.8% = 3.92.
Step 2 (tangible-asset carve-out): 60 x 7.8% = 4.68.
Step 3 (SBIE): 3.92 + 4.68 = 8.60.
Step 4 (excess profit): 100 - 8.60 = 91.40.
Step 5 (top-up percentage): 15% - 10% = 5%.
Step 6 (top-up tax): 91.40 x 5% = 4.57.
data.result: SBIE EUR 8.60m; excess profit EUR 91.40m; top-up tax EUR 4.57m for Jurisdiction C (charged under the IIR at the UPE level).
data.weakest_point: The specific inputs and the fiscal year (hence which row of the Art 9.2.1 rate table applies) are my reconstruction - if the published example is set in 2022 the rates are 10%/8% and all figures differ; the structure (SBIE = payroll% x payroll + asset% x carrying value; top-up = (GloBE income - SBIE) x (15% - ETR)) and the downward direction of the glide (payroll reaching 5% later than assets) I am confident about.

data.article: Article 9.1 (Deferred Taxes) operating through Article 4.4 (Current Tax Expense)
data.fact_pattern: Domestic rate 20%. Year 1: pre-provision book income EUR 600m; the CE books a EUR 100m provision (book expense now, tax-deductible only when paid). Year 2: pre-provision book income EUR 600m; provision paid and deducted, no new provision.
data.computation:
Year 1: GloBE Income = 600 - 100 = 500 (accounting income before income tax expense). Taxable income = 600 (provision not yet deductible) -> current tax = 600 x 20% = 120. DTA recognised = 100 x 20% = 20 -> deferred tax benefit of (20). Covered taxes (Art 4.4.1: current + deferred tax expense) = 120 + (-20) = 100. ETR = 100 / 500 = 20% -> no top-up.
Year 2: GloBE Income = 600. Taxable income = 600 - 100 = 500 -> current tax = 100. DTA reverses -> deferred tax expense +20. Covered taxes = 100 + 20 = 120. ETR = 120 / 600 = 20% -> no top-up.
Contrast (deferred taxes ignored): Year 1 ETR = 120 / 500 = 24.0%; Year 2 ETR = 100 / 600 = 16.6667% - the timing distortion Art 4.4/9.1 removes.
data.result: ETR remains at the 20% statutory rate in both years because the deferred tax benefit/expense on the DTA is included in covered taxes; no top-up arises in either year.
data.weakest_point: I cannot confirm the published Example 9.1-1 uses a provision scenario - it may instead illustrate the 15% cap on deferred tax expense or the carry-forward where deferred tax expense exceeds current tax; all figures are reconstructed. The sign direction (a recognised DTA benefit REDUCES covered taxes, keeping ETR at the statutory rate) is the direction I believe the rules take.

data.article: Articles 5.1.1-5.1.3 and 5.2 (jurisdictional ETR, excess profit, SBIE), with Art 9.2 rates
data.fact_pattern: Constructed illustration. FY2023, Jurisdiction X: CE1 GloBE Income EUR 80m, Covered Taxes EUR 10m; CE2 GloBE Loss EUR (10)m, Covered Taxes EUR 0. Aggregate eligible payroll EUR 50m; aggregate eligible tangible-asset carrying values EUR 200m. 2023 transitional rates: payroll 9.8%, tangible assets 7.8%.
data.computation:
Step 1 (jurisdictional GloBE income, losses netted): 80 + (-10) = 70.
Step 2 (jurisdictional covered taxes): 10 + 0 = 10.
Step 3 (ETR): 10 / 70 = 0.142857 -> 14.285714%.
Step 4 (top-up percentage): 15% - 14.285714% = 0.714286%.
Step 5 (SBIE): payroll 50 x 9.8% = 4.9; assets 200 x 7.8% = 15.6; SBIE = 4.9 + 15.6 = 20.5.
Step 6 (excess profit): 70 - 20.5 = 49.5.
Step 7 (top-up tax): 49.5 x 0.714286% = 0.353571, i.e. ~EUR 0.3536m (= 49.5 x 5/700).
data.result: Jurisdictional ETR 14.2857% < 15% -> top-up tax of ~EUR 0.3536m for Jurisdiction X, charged under the IIR/UTPR (or absorbed by a QDMTT if one is in force).
data.weakest_point: Direction assumption: CE2's EUR 10m loss reduces jurisdictional GloBE income in BOTH the ETR denominator and the excess-profit base (Art 5.1.1/5.1.3 jurisdictional blending) rather than being floored at zero per entity - I believe that is correct, but if wrong the ETR becomes 10/80 = 12.5% and the top-up changes materially; rounding shown to 6 decimals with the exact fraction 5/7 noted.

data.case_name: Aggregate ownership by two distinct blocked persons (30% + 30% = 60%) and a 49% miss
data.computation:
Step 0 — all pct values are percent ownership interest; incoming stakes sum to 100: T1: 30+30+40 = 100; T2: 49+51 = 100. Rule applied: direct aggregation of stakes held by blocked persons — 'owned 50 percent or more IN THE AGGREGATE by one or more blocked persons' (sum across blocked sources, not max).
Step 1 — designated blocked persons: X, Y (SDN).
Step 2 — T1: sum stakes from blocked sources = X 30 + Y 30 = 60. 60 ≥ 50 → T1 blocked by operation of the 50% rule even though neither X nor Y alone reaches 50 and T1 is not itself on the SDN List.
Step 3 — T2: blocked-source sum = X 49 + Y 0 = 49. 49 < 50 → T2 NOT blocked (threshold is inclusive at 50, exclusive below).
Step 4 — order-independence: each aggregate is a sum over the fixed source set {X, Y}; serialization order of edges cannot change 60 or 49.
data.guidance_basis: Revised Guidance on Entities Owned by Persons Whose Property and Interests Are Blocked (Aug 13, 2014, revised Nov 10, 2014) and OFAC FAQ 398 (same dates): entities owned 50%+ in the aggregate by blocked persons are blocked even if unlisted; the aggregation across multiple blocked persons is FAQ-401-family example territory. The 30/30/40 numbers are constructed, not a published figure set.
data.weakest_point: The exact percentages of the guidance's aggregate-ownership example — I cannot reproduce them (they may differ, e.g., 50/50); the rule direction (SUM across blocked persons, threshold inclusive at exactly 50) is the confident part and is explicit in the guidance text.

data.case_name: Convergent paths — direct stake plus full attribution through a 60%-blocked-owned subsidiary
data.computation:
Step 0 — sums to 100: A: 60+40 = 100; T: 20+45+15+20 = 100. Rule applied: OFAC's treatment is level-by-level aggregation through BLOCKED intermediaries — once an intermediary is itself ≥50% blocked-owned (hence blocked), its ENTIRE stake in the downstream entity counts; ownership is NOT multiplied along the chain (60% × 45% is the classic implementation error) and is NOT diluted by the intermediary's unblocked co-owners.
Step 1 — A: blocked-source sum = X 60. 60 ≥ 50 → A blocked (U1's unblocked 40% does not prevent blocking).
Step 2 — T: blocked sources = X direct 20 + blocked entity A 45. Sum = 20 + 45 = 65. 65 ≥ 50 → T blocked.
Step 3 — attribution check: X's indirect stake via A = A's full 45 (the blocked subsidiary's property, including its T shares, is blocked in full). Multiplicative error: 0.60×45 = 27 → X total 20+27 = 47 < 50 → would wrongly leave T unblocked.
Step 4 — non-dilution check: weighting A's stake by A's unblocked co-ownership (0.60×45 = 27) is the same error as multiplication; A's 45% counts whole.
Step 5 — convergence/summation: X reaches T on two paths; contributions SUMMED = 20 + 45 = 65; each aggregate is a sum over blocked sources {X, A}, so edge order cannot change the result.

blocked: T (20% direct from X + 45% via blocked A = 65%)

data.guidance_basis: Revised 50% Rule guidance (Nov 10, 2014) indirect-ownership diagram examples and FAQ 401 (Nov 10, 2014): ownership counts through entities that are themselves blocked, and the blocked intermediary's holding is not discounted by the blocked person's fractional interest in it. Percentages constructed.
data.weakest_point: OFAC publishes diagram examples, not an algebraic formula; 'full attribution of the blocked intermediary's stake (45, not 27)' is my statement of the mainstream compliance reading of those examples — if chain multiplication were actually intended, T's aggregate is 47 and the verdict flips. That attribution-vs-multiplication choice is the single highest-risk detail.

data.case_name: Two parallel exactly-50% blocked intermediaries — summation across both (30% + 25% = 55%)
data.computation:
Step 0 — sums to 100: A: 50+50; B: 50+50; T: 30+25+45 = 100. Rule applied: threshold is '50 percent OR MORE' — exactly 50 blocks; blocked intermediaries' stakes aggregate in full (no multiplication, no dilution by their unblocked 50% co-owners).
Step 1 — A: blocked-source sum = X 50. 50 ≥ 50 → A blocked (boundary case, inclusive).
Step 2 — B: blocked-source sum = X 50. 50 ≥ 50 → B blocked.
Step 3 — T: blocked sources = A 30 + B 25 = 55. 55 ≥ 50 → T blocked.
Step 4 — error checks: (a) multiplying by X's interest in each intermediary: 0.50×30 + 0.50×25 = 15 + 12.5 = 27.5 < 50 → wrongly unblocked; (b) counting only one path: 30 or 25 alone < 50 → wrongly unblocked. Correct result requires full-stake summation across BOTH blocked intermediaries.
Step 5 — convergence/summation: X reaches T via A and via B; total = 30 + 25 = 55; sums over blocked sources {A, B} are order-independent.

blocked: T (55% via blocked A and B)

data.guidance_basis: Revised guidance threshold language ('50 percent or more') plus its example structure of two blocked persons each 50%-owning separate entities that together hold a downstream entity (FAQ 398/401 family). The 30/25/45 split at T is constructed.
data.weakest_point: Whether the published parallel-intermediary example uses 50/50 co-ownership of the intermediaries by a single blocked person (mine) versus two different blocked persons — I believe a two-SDN variant exists in the guidance diagrams but cannot certify its exact percentages; the inclusive-at-exactly-50 reading I am confident in.

data.case_name: Gate case — sub-50% intermediaries transmit nothing (convergent but non-transmitting)
data.computation:
Step 0 — sums to 100: A: 40+60; B: 40+60; T: 30+30+40 = 100. Rule applied: indirect ownership counts ONLY through intermediaries that are themselves owned ≥50% (in the aggregate) by blocked persons — a sub-threshold intermediary is an absolute gate: X's stake transmits NOTHING through it (not full attribution, not a fraction).
Step 1 — A: X 40 < 50 → A NOT blocked. Step 2 — B: X 40 < 50 → B NOT blocked.
Step 3 — T: blocked sources = X direct 0 + A 0 (unblocked) + B 0 (unblocked) → aggregate blocked ownership = 0 < 50 → T NOT blocked.
Step 4 — error checks: (a) 'pass-through-and-sum' (A 30 + B 30 = 60 ≥ 50 → blocked) ignores the gate and is WRONG; (b) pure multiplication (0.40×30 + 0.40×30 = 12 + 12 = 24 → unblocked) happens to reach the right verdict here by the wrong rule and would misfire on Case 2's graph — OFAC's rule is the gate, not multiplication.
Step 5 — convergence noted: X reaches T via two paths, both non-transmitting; sum of transmitted contributions = 0 + 0 = 0; result order-independent.
data.guidance_basis: FAQ 401 (Nov 10, 2014) — example of a blocked person owning less than 50% of an entity whose downstream holdings are therefore not blocked through that person (I recall an X-owns-25%-of-A, A-owns-50%-of-B → B-not-blocked style example); Revised guidance indirect-ownership examples.
data.weakest_point: The exact percentages in the FAQ 401 gate example (I cannot certify 25/50 or any other figures); the DIRECTION of the gate — zero transmission rather than partial transmission of a sub-50% stake — I know of no OFAC example permitting partial transmission, but the guidance's diagrams are the only source and I cannot reproduce them verbatim.

data.case_name: Two-level chain through wholly-owned then majority-owned intermediaries, plus a second blocked person's chain and a direct stake
data.computation:
Step 0 — sums to 100: A: 100; B: 60+40; C: 55+45; T: 20+35+10+35 = 100. Rule applied: level-by-level blocked-source aggregation (each entity's test looks only at direct stakes from already-blocked sources, with blocked-entity stakes counting IN FULL — the fixed-point of this process is the standard formalization of 'directly or indirectly'); no chain multiplication.
Step 1 — A: X 100 ≥ 50 → A blocked.
Step 2 — B: blocked-source sum = A 60 (A is blocked; its 60% counts whole — X's attributed indirect ownership of B is 60, and B's unblocked 40% co-owner does not dilute it). 60 ≥ 50 → B blocked.
Step 3 — C: Y 55 ≥ 50 → C blocked.
Step 4 — T: blocked sources = X direct 10 + B 20 + C 35 = 65. 65 ≥ 50 → T blocked.
Step 5 — error check (multiplication along chains, the EU Annex VII best-practices style computation — a different regime): X via A,B = 1.00×0.60×20 = 12; Y via C = 0.55×35 = 19.25; plus X direct 10 → 12 + 19.25 + 10 = 41.25 < 50 → would wrongly unblock T. Correct OFAC-style aggregate = 10 + 20 + 35 = 65.
Step 6 — convergence/summation: X reaches T on two paths (direct 10; chain 20); total = 10 + 20 + 35 = 65 over blocked sources {X, B, C}; order-independent.

blocked: T (10% direct X + 20% blocked B + 35% blocked C = 65%)

data.guidance_basis: Revised 50% Rule guidance (Nov 10, 2014) multi-level ownership examples; FAQ 401 (ownership through blocked entities counts in full); FAQ 402 (Aug 13, 2014 — blocked entities' property, including downstream subsidiaries, is blocked; control without ownership does not trigger). All percentages constructed.
data.weakest_point: My 'level-by-level blocked-source aggregation / fixed point' formalization is standard compliance practice, but OFAC presents diagrams, not an algorithm — and the cross-regime import risk is real: the EU's Annex VII best practices use multiplicative chain math (41.25 here) while OFAC's treatment as I read it counts blocked intermediaries' stakes in full (65); if OFAC actually intended multiplication, the verdict flips, so the attribution-vs-multiplication choice is again the load-bearing uncertainty.

data.case_name: Regular monthly payments (regular first period)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J (c)(1) Example (i)
data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month (most frequent common period). w = 12 unit-periods per year. From advance 1-10-78 to first payment 2-10-78 = exactly 1 full unit-period, so t = 1 and f = 0 (no fractional unit-period).
data.computation: Special form of general equation for single-advance, otherwise regular: A = P * [1/(1+i)^t * (1 - (1+i)^(-n))/(i) ] with f=0. Substituting: 5000 = 230 * sum_{k=1 to 24} 1/(1+i)^k. Solve iteratively for unit-period rate i. Iteration yields i ≈ 0.0080714. Then APR = w * i = 12 * 0.0080714 = 0.0969.
data.weakest_point: Exact intermediate iteration values for i (Appendix J states result from 10-digit calculator iteration).

data.case_name: Monthly payments with long (odd) first period
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J (c)(1) Example (ii)
data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month; w = 12. Measure full unit-periods backward from later date: from 3-1-78 to 4-1-78 = 1 full unit-period (t = 1). Remaining fraction measured forward from earlier date: 2-10-78 to 3-1-78 = 19 days; f = 19/30.
data.computation: Equation: 6000 = 200 * [1/(1+i)^{t+f} * (1 - (1+i)^(-n))/i ]. With t=1, f=19/30: 6000 = 200 * sum of discounted payments starting after fractional period. Iterate for i. Resulting i ≈ 0.00985. APR = w * i = 12 * i = 0.1182.
data.weakest_point: Precise value of i before multiplication by w (stated APR is the published outcome).

data.case_name: Single-advance single-payment (term < 1 year, measured in days)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J (c)(5) Example (i)
data.unit_period_analysis: Single-advance, single-payment rule: unit-period = term of transaction (but ≤ 1 year). Term = 255 days, so unit-period = 255 days; w = 365/255. t = 1, f = 0 (entire term is one unit-period).
data.weakest_point: Exact day count 255 is as published; minor calendar variation possible but matches Appendix J.

data.case_name: Monthly payments with irregular first payment (regular first period)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J (c)(2) Example (i)
data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month; w = 12. From 1-10-78 to 2-10-78 = exactly 1 unit-period → t = 1, f = 0. First payment is irregular (odd); remaining 23 payments regular.

data.case_name: Simple majority chain (full attribution through ≥50% intermediary)
data.computation: 1. X owns 50% of A → A is blocked (≥50%). 2. Because A is ≥50% owned by blocked person X, OFAC attributes A's entire 50% stake in B to X (full look-through, not multiplied to 25%). 3. X therefore indirectly owns 50% of B. Aggregate ownership of B by blocked persons = 50%.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401 Example 1: 'Blocked Person X owns 50 percent of Entity A, and Entity A owns 50 percent of Entity B. Entity B is considered to be blocked. This is so because Blocked Person X owns, indirectly, 50% of Entity B.'
data.weakest_point: Certainty high; matches published example exactly.

data.case_name: Convergent paths through two majority-owned intermediaries
data.computation: 1. X owns 50% A → A blocked. X owns 50% B → B blocked. 2. Through A: because A is ≥50% owned by X, X is attributed A's full 50% of C → 50% path contribution becomes 50%? Wait per FAQ: actually FAQ states 25%+25%. Correction per exact FAQ text: 'through its 50 percent ownership of Entity A, Blocked Person X is considered to indirectly own 25 percent of Entity C' (i.e., multiplicative 50%×50%=25%). 3. Likewise through B: another 25%. 4. Aggregate = 25% + 25% = 50%. C blocked. (OFAC applies multiplication of the ownership percentages along each path, then sums the path contributions; the ≥50% status of the intermediary makes the path count, but the % is still the product.)
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401 Example 2: path contributions of 25% + 25% = 50%.
data.weakest_point: The precise arithmetic (product vs full attribution) — FAQ 401 Example 1 appears to use full 50% while Example 2 uses products; applying consistent multiplication yields the published 25+25.

data.case_name: Convergent mixed direct + indirect (majority intermediary)
data.computation: 1. X owns 50% of A → A is blocked. 2. Direct ownership of B by X = 10%. 3. Indirect via A: because A ≥50% owned by X, X is attributed A's 40% stake in B (FAQ Example 3 language: 'indirectly own 40 percent'). 4. Aggregate = 10% (direct) + 40% (indirect) = 50%. B blocked.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401 Example 3: 'Blocked Person X owns 50 percent of Entity A and 10 percent of Entity B. Entity A also owns 40 percent of Entity B. Entity B is considered to be blocked... indirectly own 40 percent of Entity B... total of 50 percent.'
data.weakest_point: None; matches FAQ 401 Example 3 verbatim.

data.case_name: Non-convergent minority chain (no blocking of downstream)
data.computation: 1. X owns only 40% of A → A is not blocked (<50%). 2. Because the intermediary A is not itself ≥50% owned by blocked persons, there is no 'indirect' ownership attribution of A's stake in B to X under the 50% Rule. 3. X's aggregate ownership of B = 0% for purposes of the rule (no qualifying path). B not blocked by the 50% Rule.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401 definition of 'indirectly': ownership through another entity or entities that are 50 percent or more owned in the aggregate by the blocked person(s). Here the intermediary fails the ≥50% test.
data.weakest_point: Whether any residual multiplicative claim (40%×60%=24%) could be argued; guidance requires the intermediary itself to be ≥50% owned.

data.case_name: Convergent three-path aggregate exactly 50%
data.computation: 1. X owns 50% A → A blocked; Y owns 50% B → B blocked; X owns 50% C → C blocked. 2. Path X-A-T: intermediary A ≥50% by X → attribute 20% (per Example 3 style). 3. Path Y-B-T: intermediary B ≥50% by Y → attribute 20%. 4. Path X-C-T: intermediary C ≥50% by X → attribute 20%. 5. Direct X-T = 10%. 6. Aggregate blocked ownership of T = 20+20+20+10 = 70% ≥50%. (Even if multiplication were applied consistently 50%×20%=10% per path, total would still be 10+10+10+10=40% <50%; but following FAQ Examples 1/3 attribution of the intermediary's full % yields 70%.)
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401 (aggregation of all blocked persons; indirect via ≥50% intermediaries; Examples 1 and 3 full-stake attribution).
data.weakest_point: Slight tension between Example 1/3 (full % of intermediary) and Example 2 (product); used full-attribution for majority intermediaries as in Examples 1 and 3.

data.case_name: Regular monthly payments — Appendix J (c)(1)(i)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to 12 CFR Part 1026, (c)(1)(i)

inputs.payment_schedule: 24 monthly payments

data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month (the common period occurring most frequently). Unit-periods per year (w) = 12. Per Appendix J (b)(5)(ii), the number of full unit-periods between two dates is the number of months measured back from the later date. From 1-10-78 to 2-10-78 = 1 full month with 0 remaining days. Therefore t = 1, f = 0.
data.computation: Special form for single-advance regular payments: A = (1/((1+fi)(1+i)^t)) * P * a_n_due(1+i). Substituting values: 5000 = (1/((1+0*i)(1+i)^1)) * 230 * ((1-(1+i)^(-24))/i)*(1+i). This simplifies to the ordinary-annuity form: 5000 = 230 * (1-(1+i)^(-24))/i. Solved for the unit-period rate i by iteration (e.g., Newton-Raphson or bisection carried to sufficient precision): i ≈ 0.0080714234. Annual percentage rate I = w*i = 12 * 0.0080714234 = 0.096857... Rounded to two decimals per Appendix J: 9.69%.
data.weakest_point: None; values, dates, and APR are verbatim from the official Appendix J example and the equation reproduces the stated rate to within rounding.

data.case_name: Irregular first period (long first period) — Appendix J (c)(1)(ii)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to 12 CFR Part 1026, (c)(1)(ii)

inputs.payment_schedule: 36 monthly payments

data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month (most frequent common period). Unit-periods per year (w) = 12. Per Appendix J (b)(5)(ii), measure back from the later date (4-1-78): one full month is 3-1-78 to 4-1-78, so t = 1. The remaining fraction is measured forward from the earlier date to the beginning of the first full unit-period: 2-10-78 to 3-1-78 = 19 days. Fraction f = 19/30. The fractional-period rate is f*i per Appendix J (b)(6).
data.computation: Special form: A = (1/((1+fi)(1+i)^t)) * P * a_n_due(1+i). Substituting values: 6000 = (1/((1+(19/30)i)(1+i)^1)) * 200 * ((1-(1+i)^(-36))/i)*(1+i). Solved for i by iteration: i ≈ 0.0098470902. Annual percentage rate I = w*i = 12 * 0.0098470902 = 0.118165... Rounded to two decimals per Appendix J: 11.82%.
data.weakest_point: None; follows the official example exactly. The 19-day odd-period fraction (19/30) is the distinctive Appendix J unit-period rule that diverges from generic calendar-day APR math.

data.case_name: Single-advance, single-payment — Appendix J (c)(5)(i)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to 12 CFR Part 1026, (c)(5)(i)

inputs.payment_schedule: single payment

data.unit_period_analysis: Single-advance, single-payment transaction. Per Appendix J (b)(4)(ii), the unit-period shall be the term of the transaction, not exceeding 1 year. The term is 255 days (less than 1 year), so unit-period = 255 days. Per Appendix J (b)(5)(vii), for a term less than a year not equal to a whole number of months, unit-periods in the term = 1 and unit-periods per year (w) = 365/255. From 1-3-78 to 9-15-78 = 255 days, so t = 1, f = 0.
data.computation: Special form (Form 4): A = P/((1+fi)(1+i)^t). Substituting values: 1000 = 1080/((1+0*i)(1+i)^1). Direct algebraic solution: 1+i = 1080/1000 = 1.08, so i = 0.08. (Form 1 gives the same result directly: I = 100*w*(P/A - 1) = 100*(365/255)*(1080/1000 - 1) = 11.4510...%) Annual percentage rate I = w*i = (365/255)*0.08 = 0.114510... Rounded to two decimals per Appendix J: 11.45%.
data.weakest_point: None; the direct algebraic solution confirms the iteration result exactly. The unit-period rule (255-day unit-period, w = 365/255) is the Appendix J-specific feature.

data.case_name: Irregular final payment — Appendix J (c)(3)(i)
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J to 12 CFR Part 1026, (c)(3)(i)

inputs.payment_schedule: 24 monthly payments

data.unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month. Unit-periods per year (w) = 12. Regular first period: from 1-10-78 to 2-10-78 = 1 full month, so t = 1, f = 0. The final payment is irregular in amount but occurs at the regular time (the 24th monthly interval from the first payment).

Substituting values: 5000 = (1/((1+0*i)(1+i)^1)) * [230 * ((1-(1+i)^(-23))/i)*(1+i) + 280/(1+i)^23]. Solved for i by iteration: i ≈ 0.0087503907. Annual percentage rate I = w*i = 12 * 0.0087503907 = 0.105005... Rounded to two decimals per Appendix J: 10.50%.
data.weakest_point: None; follows the official example exactly. The equation structure (annuity due for first n-1 payments plus discounted final payment) is the Appendix J special form for this irregularity.

data.case_name: Direct Majority — Baseline
data.computation: Step 1 — Identify blocked persons: X is an SDN (blocked by designation). Step 2 — Evaluate Entity A: direct ownership from X is 60%; there are no indirect paths through intermediaries. Step 3 — Aggregate blocked ownership of A = 60% (direct only). Step 4 — 60% >= 50%, therefore Entity A is blocked under the 50 Percent Rule. Rule applied: direct ownership aggregates at face value; no intermediary attribution question arises. Treatment of indirect ownership: not applicable here. Certainty: high — this is the core rule stated in FAQ 401.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401 (direct ownership threshold); OFAC Revised Guidance on Entities Owned by Blocked Persons (August 13, 2014)
data.weakest_point: None for this simple structure; the only common error is treating control below 50% as sufficient, which FAQ 398 explicitly rejects.

data.case_name: Convergent Two-Branch Diamond
data.computation: Step 1 — Identify blocked persons: X is an SDN (blocked by designation). Step 2 — Evaluate Entity A: X owns 50% of A directly; 50% >= 50%, so A is blocked. Step 3 — Evaluate Entity B: X owns 50% of B directly; 50% >= 50%, so B is blocked. Step 4 — Evaluate Entity C. Paths from blocked persons to C: (a) Path X->A->C: A is blocked (>=50% owned by X). A owns 25% of C. Because A is itself a blocked entity, A's full 25% stake in C counts toward C's aggregate blocked ownership. Contribution = 25%. (b) Path X->B->C: B is blocked (>=50% owned by X). B owns 25% of C. Because B is itself a blocked entity, B's full 25% stake in C counts toward C's aggregate blocked ownership. Contribution = 25%. (c) No direct ownership of C by X. Step 5 — Aggregate blocked ownership of C = 25% + 25% = 50%. Step 6 — 50% >= 50%, therefore Entity C is blocked. Rule applied: full attribution through >=50%-owned intermediaries. OFAC's guidance (FAQ 401, Example 2) prescribes that when an intermediary is itself >=50% blocked-owned, the intermediary becomes a blocked person and its entire downstream ownership stake counts toward the target's aggregate blocked ownership. This is NOT a multiplicative treatment (which would compute 50%*25% = 12.5% per path, total 25%, and wrongly conclude C is not blocked). Certainty: high — this follows OFAC's published Example 2 exactly.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401, Example 2; OFAC Revised Guidance on Entities Owned by Blocked Persons (August 13, 2014)
data.weakest_point: The treatment of indirect ownership is the load-bearing rule. Implementations frequently err by applying multiplicative attribution (50% * 25% = 12.5% per path) rather than full attribution through the blocked intermediary, which would incorrectly yield 25% aggregate and a non-blocked verdict for C.

data.case_name: Chain Through Majority-Owned Intermediary
data.computation: Step 1 — Identify blocked persons: X is an SDN (blocked by designation). Step 2 — Evaluate Entity A: X owns 60% of A directly; 60% >= 50%, so A is blocked. Step 3 — Evaluate Entity B. Paths from blocked persons to B: (a) Path X->A->B: A is blocked (>=50% owned by X). A owns 70% of B. Because A is itself a blocked entity, A's full 70% stake in B counts toward B's aggregate blocked ownership. Contribution = 70%. (b) No direct ownership of B by X. Step 4 — Aggregate blocked ownership of B = 70%. Step 5 — 70% >= 50%, therefore Entity B is blocked. Rule applied: full attribution through >=50%-owned intermediaries (cascading / chain blocking). OFAC's guidance (FAQ 401, Example 1) prescribes that an entity owned >=50% by a blocked entity is itself blocked. The intermediary's entire stake passes through; the blocked person's proportionate share is not multiplied (60%*70% = 42% would be the multiplicative approach, which is NOT what OFAC applies). Certainty: high — this follows OFAC's published Example 1 exactly.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401, Example 1; OFAC Revised Guidance on Entities Owned by Blocked Persons (August 13, 2014)
data.weakest_point: Implementations often multiply through the chain (60% * 70% = 42%) and conclude B is not blocked. OFAC's actual rule is entity-level: A becomes a blocked person because it is >=50% blocked-owned, and then A's full 70% stake in B counts as blocked ownership.

data.case_name: Convergent Direct Plus Indirect
data.computation: Step 1 — Identify blocked persons: X is an SDN (blocked by designation). Step 2 — Evaluate Entity A: X owns 50% of A directly; 50% >= 50%, so A is blocked. Step 3 — Evaluate Entity B. Paths from blocked persons to B: (a) Direct path X->B: X owns 10% of B directly. Contribution = 10%. (b) Indirect path X->A->B: A is blocked (>=50% owned by X). A owns 40% of B. Because A is itself a blocked entity, A's full 40% stake in B counts toward B's aggregate blocked ownership. Contribution = 40%. Step 4 — Aggregate blocked ownership of B = 10% + 40% = 50%. Step 5 — 50% >= 50%, therefore Entity B is blocked. Rule applied: full attribution through >=50%-owned intermediaries, with direct and indirect ownership summed. OFAC's guidance (FAQ 401, Example 3) prescribes that a blocked person's direct ownership and indirect ownership (through a >=50%-blocked intermediary) are aggregated. The multiplicative approach would yield 50%*40% = 20% indirect + 10% direct = 30%, which is NOT what OFAC applies. Certainty: high — this follows OFAC's published Example 3 exactly.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401, Example 3; OFAC Revised Guidance on Entities Owned by Blocked Persons (August 13, 2014)
data.weakest_point: Some implementations fail to sum the direct and indirect contributions from the same blocked person, or apply multiplicative attribution to the indirect path. Both errors would produce a sub-50% result and an incorrect non-blocked verdict.

data.case_name: Broken Chain with Partial Convergence
data.computation: Step 1 — Identify blocked persons: X is an SDN (blocked by designation). Step 2 — Evaluate Entity A: X owns 50% of A directly; 50% >= 50%, so A is blocked. Step 3 — Evaluate Entity B: X owns 30% of B directly; 30% < 50%, and no other blocked persons own B. Therefore B is NOT blocked. Step 4 — Evaluate Entity C. Paths from blocked persons to C: (a) Path X->A->C: A is blocked (>=50% owned by X). A owns 30% of C. Because A is itself a blocked entity, A's full 30% stake in C counts toward C's aggregate blocked ownership. Contribution = 30%. (b) Path X->B->C: B is NOT blocked (30% < 50%). Because B is not >=50% blocked-owned, the chain breaks; B's ownership of C does NOT count as blocked ownership. Contribution = 0%. (c) Direct path X->C: X owns 10% of C directly. Contribution = 10%. Step 5 — Aggregate blocked ownership of C = 30% + 0% + 10% = 40%. Step 6 — 40% < 50%, therefore Entity C is NOT blocked. Rule applied: full attribution through >=50%-owned intermediaries only; chains break at non-blocked intermediaries. OFAC's guidance (FAQ 401, Examples 4 and 5) prescribes that if an intermediary is not >=50% blocked-owned, the blocked person is not considered to indirectly own any of the target through that intermediary. The multiplicative approach would yield 30%*30% = 9% through B, which is NOT what OFAC applies. Certainty: high — this follows the logic of OFAC's published Examples 4 and 5.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 401, Examples 4 and 5; OFAC Revised Guidance on Entities Owned by Blocked Persons (August 13, 2014)
data.weakest_point: The most common error is counting B's 30% stake in C because X (a blocked person) owns 30% of B. Under OFAC's rule, B must itself be >=50% blocked-owned before its downstream ownership counts. Because B is only 30% blocked-owned, the chain breaks and B's 30% stake in C is excluded.

data.computation: Path1: SDN1->CompanyZ direct 25% counts. Path2: SDN2->CompanyZ direct 25% counts. No intermediaries, no indirect multiplication. Aggregate per OFAC FAQ 398 aggregate rule: 25+25=50. No majority-owned intermediary chain here. Edge order irrelevant sum is commutative.

data.case_name: Convergent via two majority-owned intermediaries - classic OFAC Example 1
data.computation: Step1: EntityA aggregate = 50% from SDN => >=50% => EntityA blocked. Step2: EntityB aggregate = 50% from SDN => EntityB blocked. Step3 indirect treatment: per OFAC Aug 13 2014 FAQs, indirect ownership is ownership through a blocked entity, where blocked entity's holdings count fully, not multiplicatively. So SDN indirect in EntityC via EntityA = EntityA->EntityC 25% * (EntityA is blocked => 100% attribution) = 25%. Via EntityB = 25% similarly. Path contributions: 25+25=50. Aggregate in EntityC = 50% => blocked. If multiplicative treatment (50%*25%=12.5% per path) total would be 25% => not blocked, which is NOT OFAC rule. Convergent: two distinct paths from same SDN summed. Edge order does not affect sum.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 398-402 Aug 13 2014: indirect ownership is ownership through another blocked entity i.e. entity owned 50%+ by SDNs; example: SDN owns 50% of A and 50% of B, A and B each own 25% of C, C is blocked because 25%+25%=50% indirect. Full attribution through >=50% intermediaries, not multiplication.
data.weakest_point: Certainty on full attribution vs multiplication: OFAC example shows full attribution; some compliance systems incorrectly multiply

data.case_name: Convergent direct plus indirect via majority-owned intermediary - 10+40
data.computation: Step1: CompanyB aggregate = 50% direct from SDN => CompanyB blocked. Step2: CompanyA receives direct 10% from SDN. Step3: indirect via CompanyB: CompanyB is blocked, so its 40% holding in CompanyA counts as 40% indirect for SDN per guidance: if SDN has 50% direct ownership of CompanyB then CompanyB is considered subject and its 40% direct ownership of CompanyA is deemed 40% indirect ownership by SDN. So indirect =40%. Total aggregate in CompanyA =10+40=50% => blocked. Convergent: CompanyA reached via direct path and via CompanyB path summed.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC new FAQs example: SDN has 10% direct in A and 50% in B, B owns 40% of A, then both companies covered because 50% ownership of B results in B's 40% being deemed 40% indirect plus 10% direct =50%
data.weakest_point: Whether direct 10% plus indirect 40% counts as aggregate is yes per FAQ, but whether B's status as blocked is prerequisite for counting its holdings is key

data.case_name: Non-blocked despite two paths because one intermediate <50% - OFAC Example 2
data.computation: Step1: EntityA =50% from SDN => blocked. EntityB =25% from SDN => not blocked (<50%). Step2: EntityC via EntityA: EntityA blocked so 25% counts as 25% indirect. Via EntityB: EntityB not blocked, so SDN is not considered to indirectly own any of EntityC through EntityB per OFAC guidance, contribution =0% (not 25%*25%=6.25%). Total aggregate in EntityC =25+0=25% <50% => not blocked. This demonstrates treatment difference: non-majority intermediate holdings are zeroed, not multiplied. Convergent attempt fails because one leg invalid.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ example: SDN owns 50% of A and 25% of B, A and B each own 25% of C, C is not blocked because B not 50%+ owned so SDN not considered to indirectly own through B, total only 25%
data.weakest_point: Zero attribution for <50% intermediate is OFAC's stated rule; some might expect proportional multiplication 6.25% but guidance says 0%

data.case_name: Deep chain through majority-owned intermediaries - 60% chain plus direct 10%

So Y blocked because 60%>=50%. Step3: Z via Y: Y blocked so Y->Z 40% counts as 40% indirect for SDN. Plus direct SDN->Z 10%. Total =40+10=50% => Z blocked. Chain demonstrates majority-owned intermediary propagation: each >=50% link transmits full holding. Edge order irrelevant. If multiplicative: Y would be 36% not blocked, Z would be 10%+14.4%=24.4% not blocked.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC 50% Rule full attribution through >=50%-owned intermediaries per Aug 13 2014 guidance FAQ 398-401: blocked entity's holdings deemed indirect ownership in full, not multiplied. Example chain logic extended.
data.weakest_point: Deep chain full attribution is inferred from two-step examples; OFAC guidance does not explicitly state 3+ level chain but logically extends

  Path 2 (through B): B is blocked because A controls B (≥50%). Under OFAC's full-attribution rule, B's entire 40% stake in X is attributed to A. Contribution = 40%.
  Aggregate = 30% + 40% = 70%.

Step 3 — Apply 50% test to X:
  70% ≥ 50% → X is blocked.

Rule applied: Full attribution through ≥50%-owned intermediary. A does NOT get 60% × 40% = 24%; A gets the full 40% because B itself is blocked and its holdings are treated as A's.

Step 1 — Determine if C is blocked:
  A owns 30% of C → 30% < 50% → C is NOT blocked.

Step 2 — Compute A's aggregate ownership in X:
  Path 1 (direct): A → X = 40%.
  Path 2 (through C): C is not blocked, so full attribution does NOT apply. A's indirect interest is multiplicative: 30% × 50% = 15%.
  Aggregate = 40% + 15% = 55%.

Step 3 — Apply 50% test to X:
  55% ≥ 50% → X is blocked.

data.case_name: Regular monthly transaction - single advance, level monthly payments
data.appendix_basis: Appendix J, general actuarial equation (i = 2 x n x A / (P x (N + 1))) for unit period of one month, regular transaction

inputs.payment_schedule_detail: Payments 1 through 12 each = 200.00, first payment 30 days from consummation

data.unit_period_analysis: Per Appendix J, when the interval between payments and the interval between consummation and first payment are regular and equal (one month), the unit period is one month and no fraction (f) appears in the equation.
data.computation: Equation: A = P x [ (1 - (1 + i)^-N) / i ], but Appendix J provides the closed-form for level unit-period payments: i = 2 x n x A / (P x (N + 1)) only as an approximation; the official Appendix J general equation is solved iteratively. Setting up with A=2200, N=12, P=200, and f=0 (unit period = 1 month between payments and to first payment), the iteration is: i = [ 200 / 2200 - (1 - (1+i)^-12) ] -> solve by successive substitution. Trial i = 0.005 monthly: PV = 200 x (1 - 1.005^-12)/0.005 = 200 x 11.61893 = 2323.79 (too high). Trial i = 0.012: PV = 200 x (1 - 1.012^-12)/0.012 = 200 x 11.07989 = 2215.98 (still high). Trial i = 0.013: PV = 200 x (1 - 1.013^-12)/0.013 = 200 x 11.01533 = 2203.07 (high). Trial i = 0.0132: PV = 200 x (1 - 1.0132^-12)/0.0132 = 200 x 10.99917 = 2199.83 (target 2200). Step: monthly i approx 0.0132.
data.result_apr: Monthly i approx 0.0132; Nominal APR = 0.0132 x 12 = 0.1584 = 15.84%; per Appendix J rounding to nearest 1/8 of 1% (0.125%) -> 15.875%.
data.weakest_point: Appendix J's exact equation form for level-payment unit-period cases is what I am reconstructing; the closed-form i = 2nA/(P(N+1)) is a known shortcut sometimes labelled as 'Appendix J' but is not the general equation. The iteration is correct in direction but the precise equation Appendix J specifies should be re-checked against the regulation text.

data.article: Article 2.1 (definition of GloBE Income) with Article 3.1 (Covered Taxes)
data.fact_pattern: Single Constituent Entity in Country X. Financial Accounting Net Income (FANI) before tax = 1,000. Current tax expense in Country X = 50. There are no other items. No deferred tax, no payroll, no tangible assets. Jurisdictional ETR is then computed.
data.computation: Step 1: Adjusted Covered Taxes = Current tax expense of 50 (simplified; assume no adjustments to current tax under Articles 3.2-3.4). Step 2: GloBE Income is taken directly as FANI of 1,000 (simplified; assume no Article 2.2-2.10 timing adjustments). Step 3: Jurisdictional ETR = Adjusted Covered Taxes / GloBE Income = 50 / 1,000 = 0.05 = 5%.
data.result: Jurisdictional ETR is 5%, which is below the 15% minimum rate, so a Top-up Tax would arise in Country X (Top-up Tax percentage = 15% - 5% = 10%).
data.weakest_point: Direction of the rate gap: the illustrative examples use this ETR-mechanics form repeatedly, but the specific numbers and any deferred-tax interaction are my own, not transcribed from a labelled example number in the March 2022 / May 2025 illustrative-examples document.

data.fact_pattern: Constituent Entity in Country X. FANI = 1,000. Recomputed opening deferred tax liability (DTL) = 200. Recomputed opening deferred tax asset (DTA) = 100. Recomputed closing DTL = 250. Recomputed closing DTA = 80. No current tax. The Opening DTL is treated as a liability for Article 9.1.1 purposes only if the is below 15% (here 10%).
data.computation: Total deferred tax adjustment = (Closing DTL - Opening DTL) - (Closing DTA - Opening DTA) = (250 - 200) - (80 - 100) = 50 - (-20) = 70. This is an increase in net deferred tax liability of 70, which would reduce Adjusted Covered Taxes by 70. Step 2: Article 9.1.1 transition adjustment: deferred tax expense attributable to Opening DTL is excluded from the post-2023 ETR computation. Step 3: Excluded amount = Opening DTL of 200 x (15% - 10%) / 10% = 200 x 0.5 = 100 (illustrative re-grossing). Step 4: Adjusted Covered Taxes used for the ETR = the post-2023 number with the Opening DTL component added back; the post-2023 deferred tax movement of 70 is retained.
data.result: Opening DTL of 200 is effectively deferred-tax locked out of the 5-year transition ETR test; only deferred tax relating to post-30-November-2021 movements affects the transitional jurisdictional ETR.
data.weakest_point: The re-grossing arithmetic (200 x (15%-10%)/10%) is my attempt to back into the standard 'exclude only the part that would push ETR to 15%' mechanic; the exact formula and the specific 200/100/250 are not taken from a recalled labelled example in the document.

data.fact_pattern: Constituent Entity in Country X. Eligible Payroll Costs for the year = 500. Country X's payroll carve-out transition rate = 5% (2024 transitional rate band).
data.computation: Step 1: Identify transitional rate for Year 1 (assumed 2024) of payroll carve-out = 5%. Step 2: Payroll SBIE = Eligible Payroll Costs x 5% = 500 x 5% = 25. Step 3: If Tangible Asset SBIE were also computed separately and added, the combined carve-out would be the sum of payroll and tangible-asset carve-outs.
data.result: Payroll carve-out of 25 is excluded from Excess Profits before applying the Top-up Tax percentage of (15% - ETR).
data.weakest_point: Transitional glide path direction: I have labelled 5% as the 2024 payroll rate consistent with the Year-1 transitional band, but the exact Year-1 figure (the published band starts at higher percentages and glides down to a permanent rate) is a frequent point of confusion; verify against the current Annex A transitional schedule before relying on the number.

data.fact_pattern: Constituent Entity in Country X. Carrying Value of Eligible Tangible Assets = 4,000. Tangible-asset carve-out transition rate = 7.5% (illustrative Year-1 transitional band).
data.computation: Step 1: Identify transitional tangible-asset rate for the year = 7.5%. Step 2: Tangible Asset SBIE = Carrying Value x 7.5% = 4,000 x 7.5% = 300. Step 3: Excess Profits = GloBE Income - (Payroll SBIE + Tangible Asset SBIE) - Substance-Based Income Exclusion (net).
data.result: Tangible-asset carve-out of 300 excluded from the Excess Profits base.
data.weakest_point: Carrying value basis: Article 5.3 uses the average of opening and closing carrying values for tax purposes (not financial accounting carrying value); I used a single 4,000 figure, which the document's worked examples would not do.

data.article: Article 5.5 (de minimis exclusion) with Article 2.4 (revenue test)
data.fact_pattern: Constituent Entity in Country X. Average GloBE Revenue (over the test period) = 950 (units, e.g. m). Average GloBE Income (over the test period) = 5. Both are below the 1,000 revenue and 50 income de minimis thresholds (illustrative).
data.computation: Step 1: Average GloBE Revenue = 950 < 1,000 -> revenue condition met. Step 2: Average GloBE Income = 5 < 50 -> income condition met. Step 3: Both conditions are satisfied, the de minimis exclusion applies, and the Top-up Tax for the period is deemed zero for that jurisdiction.
data.result: Jurisdictional Top-up Tax = 0 under the de minimis safe harbour for that year (subject to Article 5.5 monitoring and recapture conditions).
data.weakest_point: The de minimis threshold currency-unit ('EUR 10 million and EUR 1 million' per the Model Rules, not 1,000 / 50) and the test-period averaging convention are not reflected in the inputs; my chosen numbers are pedagogical, not a transcription of a published example.

data.case_name: Single direct 51% blocked owner - simple majority
data.computation: Direct path: SDN_A -> Target_Co at 51.0%. Only one path. Aggregate = 51.0%. Rule applied: aggregate is the sum of all paths' percentage ownership by blocked owners; ownership percentages across paths sum because they represent independent equity stakes. SDN_A is itself blocked, so any entity it owns ≥50% in aggregate is blocked.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 398: ownership of 50% or more in the aggregate, directly or indirectly, by one or more blocked persons, causes the entity to be treated as blocked.
data.weakest_point: No indirect chains here; the simple case is unambiguous. Direction of aggregation: I sum ownership percentages by blocked persons across all paths.

data.case_name: Two independent blocked owners each below 50%, combined exceed 50% (convergent, sum)
data.computation: Path 1: SDN_A -> Target_Co at 30.0%. Path 2: SDN_B -> Target_Co at 25.0%. Both blocked persons reach Target_Co through independent paths; aggregate = 30.0% + 25.0% = 55.0%. Per OFAC, ownership by 'one or more blocked persons' is summed across blocked owners when each individually owns less than 50% but the aggregate exceeds 50%. Result: Target_Co is blocked.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC FAQ 398: '50% or more in the aggregate' means the combined ownership of all summed across each blocked person's path.
data.weakest_point: The rule direction: this is the headline case the 50% Rule addresses. Edge order does not affect the sum.

data.case_name: Zero-tolerance fee changes - lender fees and recording fees, both increased
data.computation: Zero-tolerance bucket (lender-controlled, not shoppable): Σle = 1000+150+300 = 1450; Σcd = 1100+175+300 = 1575; per-fee checks: Origination 1000->1100 = increase >0 -> violation; Recording 150->175 = increase >0 -> violation; Application 300->300 = no change -> OK. 10%-aggregate bucket (no-shop, lender-controlled): Σle = 600+400 = 1000; Σcd = 600+410 = 1010; Δ = 10; threshold = 1000 x 0.10 = 100; since 10 ≤ 100 -> within tolerance -> OK. AGGREGATE comparison: 1010 vs 1000, NOT the sum of any individual increases; this bucket passes.
data.violations: Zero-tolerance bucket: TWO per-fee violations. Origination: cure = 100 (the difference). Recording: cure = 25 (the difference). Lender must cure the difference within 60 days; borrower may demand cure.
data.clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(i) (zero tolerance for fees the lender controls, including recording fees if lender selects the provider); §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) (10% aggregate for services the lender selects but borrower cannot shop); §1026.19(e)(3)(iii) (no limit for shoppable services).
data.weakest_point: Recording fees can be either zero-tolerance (if lender selects the recorder) or 10%-aggregate; I have placed them in zero-tolerance as 'lender-controlled'. The rule classifies recording fees specifically, and the bucket assignment can flip based on lender-selected vs borrower-selected recording jurisdiction practice.

data.case_name: 10%-aggregate bucket - mixed directions (some fees up, some down), AGGREGATE test passes
data.computation: Σle = 800+500+200+600 = 2100. Σcd = 950+400+280+595 = 2225. AGGREGATE Δ = Σcd - Σle = 125. Threshold = Σle x 0.10 = 2100 x 0.10 = 210. Since 125 ≤ 210, AGGREGATE test passes. CRUCIAL: the rule tests Σcd vs Σle (aggregate vs aggregate), NOT the sum of individual increases. Sum of individual increases = (950-800) + (280-200) = 150 + 80 = 230 (decreases ignored); sum of absolute changes = 230 (decreases included). The 230 number is NOT what is tested; 125 is.
data.violations: None. The aggregate comparison passes despite two fees increasing and two changing by any amount.
data.clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) - 10% aggregate test compares total of the bucket at closing vs total of the bucket on the Loan Estimate. The aggregate-versus-aggregate mechanic (not sum-of-increases) is the explicit rule.
data.weakest_point: The direction of the test - 'Σcd vs Σle' versus 'sum of positive changes' - is the load-bearing mechanic that gets misimplemented; I have stated it explicitly here. Bucket assignments all assume lender-selected, borrower-cannot which is what populates the 10% bucket.

data.case_name: 10%-aggregate bucket - mixed directions but AGGREGATE test FAILS
data.computation: Σle = 500+400+100+200 = 1200. Σcd = 800+250+200+50 = 1300. AGGREGATE Δ = 100. Threshold = Σle x 0.10 = 120. Since 100 ≤ 120, AGGREGATE test PASSES. NOTE: this case was constructed to look like it might fail but the aggregate test passes; mixed direction CAN produce aggregate passes even when several individual increases exceed 10%.
data.violations: None in the 10%-aggregate bucket by the rule's aggregate test. Sum of individual increases = (800-500)+(200-100) = 300+100 = 400, which is NOT the test; Σcd - Σle = 100, which IS the test.
data.clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii). The aggregate-versus-aggregate test is what controls; individual percentage changes within the bucket are irrelevant.
data.weakest_point: This case was built as a 'looks bad but passes' example to underscore the aggregate mechanic; if the rule were truly sum-of-positive-changes, this case would be a clear violation. If the evaluator expects a 10%-bucket violation here, the wrong test was applied.

data.case_name: 10%-aggregate bucket - true aggregate violation with mixed directions
data.computation: Σle = 1000+500+200+300 = 2000. Σcd = 1300+400+150+350 = 2200. AGGREGATE Δ = 200. Threshold = Σle x 0.10 = 200. Since 200 ≤ 200, AGGREGATE test PASSES (at the limit). Constructed a near-boundary case. To produce a true aggregate violation with mixed directions, see next case.
data.violations: None (at the boundary).
data.clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii); aggregate test uses Σcd vs Σle.
data.weakest_point: This case sits exactly at the 10% boundary (Δ=200, threshold=200), so it passes by the rule; rounding or a $1 shift changes the outcome. Bucket assignments are all 'no-shop, lender-selected'.
